cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Who discovered that amber rubbed with wool or silk cloth attracts light objects, and when?
cards.back: Historically the credit of discovery of the fact that amber rubbed with wool or silk cloth attracts light objects goes to Thales of Miletus, Greece, around 600 BC.
cards.quote: Historically the credit of discovery of the fact that amber rubbed with wool or silk cloth attracts light objects goes to Thales of Miletus, Greece, around 600 BC.
reasons: review:Historical trivia (Thales, 600 BC); not a CUET-tested point.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: In the rubbed glass rod and silk observation, what do unlike charges acquired by the objects do to each other's effect?
cards.back: unlike charges acquired by the objects neutralise or nullify each other's effect.
cards.quote: It just tells us that unlike charges acquired by the objects neutralise or nullify each other's effect.
reasons: review:Front points at 'the rubbed glass rod and silk observation' the student cannot see; the answer is explanatory aside, low exam value.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: What are conductors?
cards.back: Those which allow electricity to pass through them easily are called conductors.
cards.quote: Those which allow electricity to pass through them easily are called conductors.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Which charges inside a conductor are comparatively free to move through the material?
cards.back: Those which allow electricity to pass through them easily are called conductors. They have electric charges (electrons) that are comparatively free to move inside the material.
cards.quote: Those which allow electricity to pass through them easily are called conductors. They have electric charges (electrons) that are comparatively free to move inside the material.
reasons: review:Back repeats the def-conductors sentence verbatim (same first sentence); the extra fact (free electrons) is already covered, so redundant.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Give NCERT's examples of conductors (three kinds).
cards.back: Metals, human and animal bodies and earth are conductors.
cards.quote: Metals, human and animal bodies and earth are conductors.
reasons: review:Open-ended: front says 'NCERT's examples' and a student can validly name copper, silver, water etc.; not one right answer from the front alone.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: It is not possible to create or destroy ____ charge carried by any isolated system although the charge carrying particles may be created or destroyed in a process.
cards.back: It is not possible to create or destroy net charge carried by any isolated system although the charge carrying particles may be created or destroyed in a process.
cards.quote: It is not possible to create or destroy net charge carried by any isolated system although the charge carrying particles may be created or destroyed in a process.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Who was Coulomb and how did his career begin?
cards.back: Coulomb, a French physicist, began his career as a military engineer in the West Indies.
cards.quote: Coulomb, a French physicist, began his career as a military engineer in the West Indies.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: In which year did Coulomb arrive at the inverse square law?
cards.back: He thus arrived in 1785 at the inverse square law relation, now known as Coulomb's law.
cards.quote: He thus arrived in 1785 at the inverse square law relation, now known as Coulomb's law.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Who anticipated Coulomb's law before him?
cards.back: The law had been anticipated by Priestley and also by Cavendish earlier, though Cavendish never published his results.
cards.quote: The law had been anticipated by Priestley and also by Cavendish earlier, though Cavendish never published his results.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: What else did Coulomb find about magnetic poles?
cards.back: Coulomb also found the inverse square law of force between unlike and like magnetic poles.
cards.quote: Coulomb also found the inverse square law of force between unlike and like magnetic poles.
reasons: review:Side remark on magnetic poles, off the chapter's tested core.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Define the electric field due to a charge Q at a point in space.
cards.back: Thus, the electric field due to a charge Q at a point in space may be defined as the force that a unit positive charge would experience if placed at that point.
cards.quote: Thus, the electric field due to a charge Q at a point in space may be defined as the force that a unit positive charge would experience if placed at that point.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Why does a charged comb attract uncharged pieces of paper?
cards.back: the charged comb `polarises' the piece of paper, i.e., induces a net dipole moment in the direction of field. Further, the electric field due to the comb is not uniform. This non-uniformity of the field makes a dipole to experience a net force on it.
cards.quote: the charged comb `polarises' the piece of paper, i.e., induces a net dipole moment in the direction of field. Further, the electric field due to the comb is not uniform. This non-uniformity of the field makes a dipole to experience a net force on it.

source.section: Dipole in a Uniform External Field

reasons: review:Back starts lowercase mid-sentence and carries extraction artefact `polarises' (backtick quote); NCERT prints 'polarises' with proper quotes.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Name the types of charge density defined for a continuous charge distribution.
cards.back: linear, surface and volume charge densities
cards.quote: Definition of linear, surface and volume charge densities.
cards.note: NCERT defines the surface, linear and volume charge densities for continuous charge distributions.
reasons: review:Quote is a figure caption (Fig 1.21), not NCERT's classification statement; names only, no definitions, so not a faithful Types card.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Since the field is everywhere radial, flux through the two ends of the cylindrical Gaussian surface is ____.
cards.back: Since the field is everywhere radial, flux through the two ends of the cylindrical Gaussian surface is zero.
cards.quote: Since the field is everywhere radial, flux through the two ends of the cylindrical Gaussian surface is zero.
reasons: review:Derivation step of the infinite-wire case; the tested part is the result, not this step.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Note that the above application of the Gauss' law has brought out an additional fact: E is ____ of x also.
cards.back: Note that the above application of the Gauss' law has brought out an additional fact: E is independent of x also.
cards.quote: Note that the above application of the Gauss' law has brought out an additional fact: E is independent of x also.
reasons: review:Derivation aside that depends on the figure and symbol x; not a stand-alone memory point. x is undefined on the card (relies on the sheet figure).

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: For a finite large planar sheet, Eq. (1.33) is approximately true in the ____ regions of the planar sheet, away from the ends.
cards.back: For a finite large planar sheet, Eq. (1.33) is approximately true in the middle regions of the planar sheet, away from the ends.
cards.quote: For a finite large planar sheet, Eq. (1.33) is approximately true in the middle regions of the planar sheet, away from the ends.
reasons: review:Refers to Eq. (1.33), which is not on the card; meaningless without it.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: A thin uniformly charged shell acts, outside, as if its charge were at the centre. Which solid body gives the same result?
cards.back: The same result is true for a solid sphere of uniform volume charge density.
cards.quote: The same result is true for a solid sphere of uniform volume charge density.
reasons: review:'Which solid body' is ambiguous: a charged solid conducting sphere (charge on surface) also acts like the shell; NCERT's answer needs 'uniform volume charge density' which the front does not state.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: What is an electric dipole?
cards.back: an electric dipole consists of two charges q and −q separated by a (small) distance 2a. Its total charge is zero.
cards.quote: an electric dipole consists of two charges q and −q separated by a (small) distance 2a. Its total charge is zero.

source.section: Potential due to an Electric Dipole

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: For a system of two charges q1 and q2, when is the potential energy positive?
cards.back: If q1q2 > 0, potential energy is positive.
cards.quote: If q1q2 > 0, potential energy is positive.

source.section: Potential Energy of a System of Charges

cards.note: q1q2 > 0 means like charges; the force between them is repulsive.
reasons: review:subscripts lost: q1 and q2 and 'q1q2' read as flattened symbols (product of two charges is not recoverable as plain text)

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Formula: potential energy of a dipole moment p in a uniform electric field E.
cards.back: −p.E
cards.quote: The potential energy of a dipole moment p in a uniform electric field E is −p.E.

source.section: Potential Energy of a Dipole in an External Field

cards.note: p and E are vectors; p.E is their dot product (scalar product).
reasons: review:relation depends on vector arrows and the dot-product sign lost in extraction ('-p.E'); state in words or skip

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Ordinary rubber is an insulator. Why are aircraft tyres made slightly conducting?
cards.back: To enable them to conduct charge (produced by friction) to the ground; as too much of static electricity accumulated may result in spark and result in fire.
cards.quote: To enable them to conduct charge (produced by friction) to the ground; as too much of static electricity accumulated may result in spark and result in fire.
reasons: review:worked-example case filler (aircraft tyres), low exam value

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: What is the difference between a dielectric and a conductor in how charges move in an external field?
cards.back: In a dielectric, this free movement of charges is not possible.
cards.quote: In a dielectric, this free movement of charges is not possible.
cards.note: In a conductor free charges move until the net field inside is zero; a dielectric has no free movement.
reasons: review:front asks for dielectric vs conductor but back names neither conductor behaviour nor an antecedent for 'this free movement'; not self-contained

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Name examples of non-polar molecules.
cards.back: Examples of non-polar molecules are oxygen (O2) and hydrogen (H2) molecules which, because of their symmetry, have no dipole moment.
cards.quote: Examples of non-polar molecules are oxygen (O2) and hydrogen (H2) molecules which, because of their symmetry, have no dipole moment.
reasons: review:O2 and H2 subscripts flattened to plain digits; 'name examples' is open-ended (N2, CO2 also valid)

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Name examples of polar molecules.
cards.back: An ionic molecule such as HCl or a molecule of water (H2O) are examples of polar molecules.
cards.quote: An ionic molecule such as HCl or a molecule of water (H2O) are examples of polar molecules.
reasons: review:H2O subscript flattened to plain digit; 'name examples' is open-ended (NH3 etc. also valid)

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: How big is a farad in practice?
cards.back: In practice, a farad is a very big unit
cards.quote: In practice, a farad is a very big unit
reasons: review:'a very big unit' is vague low-value recall; the useful part (microfarad, nanofarad, picofarad) is not on the card

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Formula: capacitance C with a dielectric filling the gap, in terms of the vacuum value C0.
cards.back: C = KC0 where K is the dielectric constant of the insulating substance.
cards.quote: C = KC0 where K is the dielectric constant of the insulating substance.
cards.note: C0 is the capacitance with no medium (vacuum).
reasons: review:C0 subscript flattened to 'C0' so 'C = KC0' is garbled in plain text; state in words (capacitance increases by the factor K) or skip

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Capacitors C1 and C2 in series: how does the total potential drop across the combination arise?
cards.back: The total potential drop V across the combination is the sum of the potential drops V1 and V2 across C1 and C2, respectively.
cards.quote: The total potential drop V across the combination is the sum of the potential drops V1 and V2 across C1 and C2, respectively.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Formula: total capacitance of capacitors in parallel.
cards.back: C = C1 + C2 + C3 + ... where C1, C2, C3... are individual capacitances.
cards.quote: In the parallel combination, the total capacitance C is: C = C1 + C2 + C3 + ... where C1, C2, C3... are individual capacitances.
reasons: review:subscripts lost: C1, C2, C3 flattened; 'C = C1 + C2 + C3' not reliable as plain text; state in words (total capacitance is the sum)

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Order of current carried by an average lightning and by our nerves?
cards.back: An average lightning carries currents of the order of tens of thousands of amperes and at the other extreme, currents in our nerves are in microamperes.
cards.quote: An average lightning carries currents of the order of tens of thousands of amperes and at the other extreme, currents in our nerves are in microamperes.
reasons: review:Magnitude trivia (lightning, nerves); low exam value

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: What is the average velocity of electrons moving in a conductor under an electric field called?
cards.back:
Drift velocity
the electrons move with an average velocity which is independent of time, although electrons are accelerated. This is the phenomenon of drift
cards.quote: It tells us that the electrons move with an average velocity which is independent of time, although electrons are accelerated. This is the phenomenon of drift and the velocity vd in Eq. (3.17) is called the drift velocity.

source.section: Drift of electrons and the origin of resistivity

reasons: review:Back is not a substring of the quote: it adds a 'Drift velocity' line and cuts the sentence before the naming clause (vd in Eq. 3.17 is called the drift velocity); quote also carries flattened subscript 'vd'.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: The assertion that V = IR is a statement of Ohm's law is ____.
cards.back: The assertion that V = IR is a statement of Ohm's law is not true.
cards.quote: The assertion that V = IR is a statement of Ohm's law is not true.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Nichrome, manganin and constantan are widely used in what, since their resistance changes very little with temperature?
cards.back: Manganin and constantan have similar properties. These materials are thus widely used in wire bound standard resistors since their resistance values would change very little with temperatures.
cards.quote: Manganin and constantan have similar properties. These materials are thus widely used in wire bound standard resistors since their resistance values would change very little with temperatures.
reasons: review:Front names Nichrome but quote starts at 'Manganin and constantan...'; back's 'These materials' has its antecedent outside the quote.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Which part of a bulb does ohmic power heat to incandescence?
cards.back: the coil of an electric bulb
cards.quote: It is this power which heats up, for example, the coil of an electric bulb to incandescence, radiating out heat and light.
reasons: review:Illustrative example of heating; low-value filler

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: What is the reason for the high voltage danger signs on power transmission lines?
cards.back: these wires carry current at enormous values of V and this is the reason for the high voltage danger signs on transmission lines
cards.quote: these wires carry current at enormous values of V and this is the reason for the high voltage danger signs on transmission lines
reasons: review:Trivia about danger signs; the exam point (high V transmission cuts I2R loss) is not what the card asks.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: The emf of a cell is the potential difference between its electrodes under what condition?
cards.back: the potential difference between the positive and negative electrodes in an open circuit, i.e., when no current is flowing through the cell
cards.quote: the potential difference between the positive and negative electrodes in an open circuit, i.e., when no current is flowing through the cell
reasons: review:Kind is definition but front is not 'Define/What is emf' as spec requires and back is a lowercase mid-sentence fragment; emf definition should be 'must'.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Why is the maximum allowed current in most cells kept much lower than the maximum current that can be drawn?
cards.back: in most cells the maximum allowed current is much lower than this to prevent permanent damage to the cell.
cards.quote: However, in most cells the maximum allowed current is much lower than this to prevent permanent damage to the cell.
reasons: review:Low-value explanatory aside; back has dangling 'than this' (Imax = e/r not in the card).

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Which German physicist, known for spectroscopy, gave the first and second rules for circuits?
cards.back:
Gustav Robert Kirchhoff
Mainly known for his development of spectroscopy, he also made many important contributions to mathematical physics, among them, his first and second rules for circuits.
cards.quote: Mainly known for his development of spectroscopy, he also made many important contributions to mathematical physics, among them, his first and second rules for circuits.
reasons: review:Biography-box trivia (spectroscopy); the name and 'German' in front/back are not in the quote; not an exam point.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Ohm was led to his law by an analogy with heat conduction: what are the electric field and current analogous to?
cards.back: the electric field is analogous to the temperature gradient, and the electric current is analogous to the heat flow
cards.quote: Ohm was led to his law by an analogy between the conduction of heat: the electric field is analogous to the temperature gradient, and the electric current is analogous to the heat flow.
reasons: review:From the Ohm biography box; heat-flow analogy is historical trivia, not CUET-tested.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Of special interest, is the case of a ____ where the resistors are such that Ig = 0.
cards.back: Of special interest, is the case of a balanced bridge where the resistors are such that Ig = 0.
cards.quote: Of special interest, is the case of a balanced bridge where the resistors are such that Ig = 0.
reasons: review:Front carries 'Ig' with the subscript flattened to plain text (I sub g)

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Keeping known resistances R1 and R2 in the first and second arm of the bridge, we go on varying R3 till the galvanometer shows a ____.
cards.back: Keeping known resistances R1 and R2 in the first and second arm of the bridge, we go on varying R3 till the galvanometer shows a null deflection.
cards.quote: Keeping known resistances R1 and R2 in the first and second arm of the bridge, we go on varying R3 till the galvanometer shows a null deflection.
reasons: review:Front carries R1, R2, R3 with subscripts flattened to plain digits

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: The deflection increases on increasing the current or bringing the needle ____ to the wire.
cards.back: The deflection increases on increasing the current or bringing the needle closer to the wire.
cards.quote: The deflection increases on increasing the current or bringing the needle closer to the wire.
reasons: review:Case-story detail (deflection grows with current or nearness); not a memory item CUET tests

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: For which directions of velocity relative to B does the magnetic force on a moving charge vanish?
cards.back: field vanish (become zero) if velocity and magnetic field are parallel or anti-parallel.
cards.quote: field vanish (become zero) if velocity and magnetic field are parallel or anti-parallel.
reasons: review:Back begins mid-sentence ('field vanish ...') with the subject lost, so it reads garbled

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Formula: radius r of the circular path of a charge q (mass m, speed v) moving perpendicular to a uniform magnetic field B.
cards.back: r = m v / qB
cards.quote: r = m v / qB
reasons: review:Formula r = mv/qB: NCERT prints a fraction bar; plain text 'm v / qB' flattens it and can read as (mv/q)B

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: What is the radius of the helix?
cards.back: The radius of the circular component of motion is called the radius of the helix.
cards.quote: The radius of the circular component of motion is called the radius of the helix.
reasons: review:Trivial naming of the helix radius; not worth a card

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Biot-Savart law: in which direction does the field dB of a current element dl at displacement r point?
cards.back: Its direction is perpendicular to the plane containing dl and r .
cards.quote: Its direction is perpendicular to the plane containing dl and r .
cards.note: dl is the current element and r the displacement vector from it to the point P; dB is the field it produces there.
reasons: review:Notation: dl and r are bold vectors on the printed page; extraction flattened them (stray 'r .'), so plain text cannot show they are vectors. Back also opens with dangling 'Its'.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: A current loop's field lines: which sides of the loop act as north and south poles of a magnet?
cards.back: The upper side of the loop may be thought of as the north pole and the lower side as the south pole of a magnet.
cards.quote: The upper side of the loop may be thought of as the north pole and the lower side as the south pole of a magnet.

source.section: Magnetic Field on the Axis of a Circular Current Loop

reasons: review:Answer 'upper side north, lower side south' depends on Fig. 4.10 and the current direction; meaningless without the figure

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: State Ampere's circuital law (sum of tangential field component times element length around a boundary).
cards.back: All such products are added together. We consider the limit as the lengths of elements get smaller and their number gets larger. The sum then tends to an integral. Ampere's law states that this integral is equal to μ0 times the total current passing through the surface
cards.quote: All such products are added together. We consider the limit as the lengths of elements get smaller and their number gets larger. The sum then tends to an integral. Ampere's law states that this integral is equal to μ0 times the total current passing through the surface
reasons: review:Back starts mid-passage at 'All such products' (antecedent missing) and the integral expression was lost in extraction; not a self-contained statement of the law

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: The field that normally can depend on ____ depends only on one: r.
cards.back: The field that normally can depend on three coordinates depends only on one: r.
cards.quote: The field that normally can depend on three coordinates depends only on one: r.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: The expression for the magnetic field of a straight wire provides a theoretical justification to ____.
cards.back: The expression for the magnetic field of a straight wire provides a theoretical justification to Oersted's experiments.
cards.quote: The expression for the magnetic field of a straight wire provides a theoretical justification to Oersted's experiments.
reasons: review:Filler remark that the formula justifies Oersted's experiments; not a CUET fact

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Field of an infinitely long straight current-carrying wire: when does the field tend to blow up?
cards.back: Another interesting point to note is that even though the wire is infinite, the field due to it at a non-zero distance is not infinite. It tends to blow up only when we come very close to the wire.
cards.quote: Another interesting point to note is that even though the wire is infinite, the field due to it at a non-zero distance is not infinite. It tends to blow up only when we come very close to the wire.
reasons: review:NCERT's 'another interesting point' aside; low exam value, vague one-clause answer (very close to the wire).

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Note that there are ____ distinct right-hand rules: One which gives the direction of B on the axis of current-loop and the other which gives direction of B for a straight conducting wire.
cards.back: Note that there are two distinct right-hand rules: One which gives the direction of B on the axis of current-loop and the other which gives direction of B for a straight conducting wire.
cards.quote: Note that there are two distinct right-hand rules: One which gives the direction of B on the axis of current-loop and the other which gives direction of B for a straight conducting wire.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: ____ wires are used for winding so that turns are insulated from each other.
cards.back: Enamelled wires are used for winding so that turns are insulated from each other.
cards.quote: Enamelled wires are used for winding so that turns are insulated from each other.
reasons: review:Enamelled-wire detail is construction trivia, not a tested point

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Formula: magnitude of the field B inside a long solenoid carrying a current I.
cards.back: B = μ0nI where n is the number of turns per unit length.
cards.quote: B = μ0nI where n is the number of turns per unit length.
reasons: review:Formula B = mu0 nI depends on the subscript in mu0 which extraction flattened to a plain digit

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Define the ampere (SI unit of current).
cards.back: The ampere is the value of that steady current which, when maintained in each of the two very long, straight, parallel conductors of negligible cross-section, and placed one metre apart in vacuum, would produce on each of these conductors a force
cards.quote: The ampere is the value of that steady current which, when maintained in each of the two very long, straight, parallel conductors of negligible cross-section, and placed one metre apart in vacuum, would produce on each of these conductors a force

source.section: Force Between Two Parallel Currents, the Ampere

cards.note: The force is 2 x 10^-7 newton per metre of length of each conductor.
reasons: review:Definition of the ampere is truncated at 'a force'; NCERT's sentence continues with the value (2 x 10^-7 newtons per metre of length), lost here. Incomplete definition

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Define the magnetic moment m of a current loop of area A carrying a current I.
cards.back: We define the magnetic moment of the current loop as, m=IA
cards.quote: We define the magnetic moment of the current loop as, m=IA

source.section: Torque on Current Loop, Magnetic Dipole

cards.note: Unit of magnetic moment: ampere metre squared (A m^2).
reasons: review:m=IA: m and A are vectors in NCERT (bold) and the vector marking is lost; reads as magnitude only

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Formula: magnetic moment of a planar loop of N closely wound turns, current I, area A.
cards.back: A planar loop carrying a current I, having N closely wound turns, and an area A possesses a magnetic moment m where, m=NIA
cards.quote: A planar loop carrying a current I, having N closely wound turns, and an area A possesses a magnetic moment m where, m=NIA
reasons: review:m=NIA: vector notation for m and A lost in extraction; reads as magnitude only

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: A planar current loop is equivalent to what?
cards.back: a planar current loop is equivalent to a magnetic dipole of dipole moment m = I A, which is the analogue of electric dipole moment p.
cards.quote: a planar current loop is equivalent to a magnetic dipole of dipole moment m = I A, which is the analogue of electric dipole moment p.

source.section: Circular Current Loop as a Magnetic Dipole

reasons: review:Contains 'm = I A' with the vector marking on m and A lost; also begins mid-sentence in lowercase

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: The equivalent of electric charges, i.e., ____, are not known to exist.
cards.back: The equivalent of electric charges, i.e., magnetic monopoles, are not known to exist.
cards.quote: The equivalent of electric charges, i.e., magnetic monopoles, are not known to exist.

source.section: Circular Current Loop as a Magnetic Dipole

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: A current flows in the coil of a moving coil galvanometer, which is free to rotate about a fixed axis. What acts on the coil?
cards.back: When a current flows through the coil, a torque acts on it.
cards.quote: When a current flows through the coil, a torque acts on it.
reasons: review:Front 'What acts on the coil?' also fits a magnetic force; and the card is trivial. The exam-worthy MCG point is that the torque is proportional to current (deflection), not that a torque acts.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Ammeter with a small shunt resistance: how large is the effect of introducing the instrument into the circuit?
cards.back: If rs has small value, in relation to the resistance of the rest of the circuit Rc, the effect of introducing the measuring instrument is also small and negligible.
cards.quote: If rs has small value, in relation to the resistance of the rest of the circuit Rc, the effect of introducing the measuring instrument is also small and negligible.
cards.note: rs (r with subscript s) is the shunt resistance and Rc (R with subscript c) is the resistance of the rest of the circuit.
reasons: review:Notation: back uses rs and Rc, which are subscripted r_s and R_c in the book; subscripts lost in plain text so symbols read as garbled.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: On switching to a frame moving with the charge's instantaneous velocity v, what happens to the magnetic part of the Lorentz force?
cards.back: If one switches to a frame with instantaneous velocity v, the magnetic part of the force vanishes.
cards.quote: If one switches to a frame with instantaneous velocity v, the magnetic part of the force vanishes.
reasons: review:Points to Ponder relativity remark about frame change; not in the CUET unit list and not exam-tested; poor use of student memory.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: NCERT's properties of magnets: out of which metal and its alloys is it possible to make magnets?
cards.back: It is possible to make magnets out of iron and its alloys.
cards.quote: It is possible to make magnets out of iron and its alloys.
reasons: review:Trivial intro line; front's 'NCERT's properties of magnets' points at unseen text, and cobalt/nickel also make magnets so 'which metal' is not a single answer.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: The word magnet is derived from the name of an island in Greece called ____ where magnetic ore deposits were found, as early as 600 BC.
cards.back: The word magnet is derived from the name of an island in Greece called magnesia where magnetic ore deposits were found, as early as 600 BC.
cards.quote: The word magnet is derived from the name of an island in Greece called magnesia where magnetic ore deposits were found, as early as 600 BC.
reasons: review:Word origin of 'magnet' (Magnesia) is historical trivia, not an exam point.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Who is credited with the discovery that moving charges or electric currents produce magnetic fields?
cards.back: In the previous chapter we have learned that moving charges or electric currents produce magnetic fields. This discovery, which was made in the early part of the nineteenth century is credited to Oersted, Ampere, Biot and Savart, among others.
cards.quote: In the previous chapter we have learned that moving charges or electric currents produce magnetic fields. This discovery, which was made in the early part of the nineteenth century is credited to Oersted, Ampere, Biot and Savart, among others.
reasons: review:History credit line; 'among others' means no single right answer (Oersted, Ampere, Biot, Savart); low exam value.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: What pattern of iron filings is observed around a current carrying solenoid?

the photoelectric current is directly proportional to the intensity of incident light
the stopping potential is independent of its intensity

Above the threshold frequency, the stopping potential or equivalently the maximum kinetic energy of the emitted photoelectrons increases linearly with the frequency of the incident radiation, but is independent of its intensity (Fig. 11.5). (iv) The photoelectric emission is an instantaneous process without any apparent time lag (~10– 9 s or less), even when the incident radiation is made exceedingly dim.
